title: "tsconfig Explained"
summary: "Every TypeScript project has a tsconfig.json that decides how strict the checker is, which JavaScript version comes out, which files are included and where the output goes. Learn from zero what the important options really do, by changing them one at a time and watching tsc's real output: target and lib, module and import extensions, rootDir, outDir and include, the strict family and noUncheckedIndexedAccess, declarations and source maps, noEmit, extends, --showConfig, and why paths aliases need help at runtime."
level: beginner
minutes: 35
prerequisites: ["Basic Types & Annotations", "Modules (import/export)"]
tags: ["TypeScript", "Tools"]

<BigIdea>
<Tr>
<En>
`tsconfig.json` is the **settings file** for the TypeScript compiler. When you run `tsc` (or when VS Code, Next.js or Vite check your code), they read it to answer four questions. **Which files?** (`include`, `exclude`, `rootDir`). **How strict?** (`strict` and friends like `noUncheckedIndexedAccess`). **What JavaScript should come out?** (`target` for the language version, `module` for the import style, `lib` for which built-in APIs exist, like `document` in browsers). **Where does the output go, and what else is produced?** (`outDir`, `declaration`, `sourceMap`, or `noEmit` when another tool builds the code). You rarely write a tsconfig from scratch: frameworks generate one, and `tsc --init` makes a good starting point. But when you see an error like "Cannot find name 'document'" or "Relative import paths need explicit file extensions", the fix is in this file, so it pays to know what each option really does.
</En>
<Ur>
`tsconfig.json` TypeScript compiler ki **settings file** hai. Jab aap `tsc` chalate hain (ya jab VS Code, Next.js ya Vite aap ka code check karte hain), wo ise chaar sawalon ke jawab ke liye parhte hain. **Kaun si files?** (`include`, `exclude`, `rootDir`). **Kitni sakhti?** (`strict` aur `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` jaise saathi). **Kaun sa JavaScript nikle?** (zabaan ke version ke liye `target`, import ke andaaz ke liye `module`, kaun si built-in APIs maujood hain us ke liye `lib`, jaise browsers me `document`). **Output kahan jaye, aur aur kya bane?** (`outDir`, `declaration`, `sourceMap`, ya `noEmit` jab koi aur tool code banata ho). Aap shaayad hi kabhi tsconfig shuru se likhenge: frameworks ek bana dete hain, aur `tsc --init` achha aaghaz deta hai. Magar jab "Cannot find name 'document'" ya "Relative import paths need explicit file extensions" jaisa error dikhe, hal isi file me hota hai, isliye har option ka asal kaam jaanna faidemand hai.
</Ur>
</Tr>
</BigIdea>

## At a glance

<Glance>
<What>
<Tr>
<En>

| Group | Option | What it controls |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Files | `include` / `exclude` / `files` | which `.ts` files belong to the project |
| | `rootDir` / `outDir` | where sources live / where JavaScript is written |
| Language | `target` | JavaScript version of the output (`es2022`…) |
| | `lib` | built-in types available (`es2022`, `dom`…) |
| | `module` / `moduleResolution` | import style and how imports are found |
| | `jsx` | how `.tsx` is handled (`react-jsx`, `preserve`) |
| Checking | `strict` | turns on all the important safety checks |
| | `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` | `obj[key]` might be `undefined` |
| | `noUnusedLocals`, `noImplicitReturns`… | style checks |
| Output | `declaration` | write `.d.ts` type files (for libraries) |
| | `sourceMap` | map output back to `.ts` for debugging |
| | `noEmit` | only check, write nothing |
| Other | `extends` | inherit settings from another config |
| | `paths` | import aliases like `@/lib/db` |
| | `skipLibCheck` | don't type-check `node_modules` `.d.ts` files |

</En>
<Ur>

| Giroh | Option | Kya control karta hai |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Files | `include` / `exclude` / `files` | kaun si `.ts` files project ka hissa hain |
| | `rootDir` / `outDir` | sources kahan hain / JavaScript kahan likha jaye |
| Zabaan | `target` | output ka JavaScript version (`es2022`…) |
| | `lib` | kaun si built-in types maujood hain (`es2022`, `dom`…) |
| | `module` / `moduleResolution` | import ka andaaz aur imports kaise dhoondhe jayen |
| | `jsx` | `.tsx` kaise sambhali jaye (`react-jsx`, `preserve`) |
| Checking | `strict` | tamam ahem hifazati checks on karta hai |
| | `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` | `obj[key]` `undefined` ho sakta hai |
| | `noUnusedLocals`, `noImplicitReturns`… | style checks |
| Output | `declaration` | `.d.ts` type files likho (libraries ke liye) |
| | `sourceMap` | debugging ke liye output ko `.ts` se milao |
| | `noEmit` | sirf check, kuch na likho |
| Deegar | `extends` | doosri config se settings virse me lo |
| | `paths` | `@/lib/db` jaise import aliases |
| | `skipLibCheck` | `node_modules` ki `.d.ts` files type-check na karo |

</Ur>
</Tr>
</What>
<Why>
<Tr>
<En>

- **The same code can pass or fail** depending on these settings; knowing them explains "it works on my machine" type errors.
- **Wrong `target` or `lib`** means confusing errors or output that doesn't run where you deploy.
- **Strictness is where TypeScript's value comes from**: a project with `strict: false` misses whole classes of bugs.
- **Build tools rely on it**: Next.js, Vite, Jest and ESLint all read your tsconfig.

</En>
<Ur>

- **Ek hi code in settings ke hisaab se paas ya fail** ho sakta hai; inhen jaanna "mere computer par chalta hai" wale type errors samjhata hai.
- **Ghalat `target` ya `lib`** ka matlab ulajhane wale errors ya aisa output jo deploy ki jagah par na chale.
- **TypeScript ki asal qeemat sakhti se aati hai**: `strict: false` wala project bugs ki poori qismen chhor deta hai.
- **Build tools is par bharosa karte hain**: Next.js, Vite, Jest aur ESLint sab aap ki tsconfig parhte hain.

</Ur>
</Tr>
</Why>
<When>
<Tr>
<En>

| Project | Typical setup |
| --- | --- |
| Next.js / Vite app | framework's tsconfig, `noEmit: true` (the bundler builds), `moduleResolution: "bundler"`, `paths` for `@/` |
| Node.js API compiled with tsc | `module: "nodenext"`, `outDir: "dist"`, `rootDir: "src"`, `.js` extensions in imports |
| Node.js run directly (`node file.ts`) | `noEmit`, `erasableSyntaxOnly`, `module: "nodenext"`, `allowImportingTsExtensions` |
| Library published to npm | `declaration: true`, `declarationMap`, `outDir` |
| Monorepo | a shared `tsconfig.base.json` + `extends` in each package |

</En>
<Ur>

| Project | Aam setup |
| --- | --- |
| Next.js / Vite app | framework ki tsconfig, `noEmit: true` (bundler banata hai), `moduleResolution: "bundler"`, `@/` ke liye `paths` |
| tsc se compile hone wali Node.js API | `module: "nodenext"`, `outDir: "dist"`, `rootDir: "src"`, imports me `.js` extensions |
| Seedha chalne wala Node.js (`node file.ts`) | `noEmit`, `erasableSyntaxOnly`, `module: "nodenext"`, `allowImportingTsExtensions` |
| npm par shaya hone wali library | `declaration: true`, `declarationMap`, `outDir` |
| Monorepo | mushtarka `tsconfig.base.json` + har package me `extends` |

</Ur>
</Tr>
</When>
<How>
<Tr>
<En>

1. Start from your framework's generated file, or run `npx tsc --init`.
2. Keep `strict: true` from day one.
3. Set `target`/`lib` for where the code runs, and `module` for how it's loaded.
4. Run `npx tsc --showConfig` to see the final, merged settings when something is confusing.

</En>
<Ur>

1. Apne framework ki banayi file se shuru karein, ya `npx tsc --init` chalayen.
2. Pehle din se `strict: true` rakhein.
3. Code jahan chalta hai us ke liye `target`/`lib`, aur jaise load hota hai us ke liye `module` set karein.
4. Jab kuch ulajhane wala ho to aakhri, mili hui settings dekhne ke liye `npx tsc --showConfig` chalayen.

</Ur>
</Tr>
</How>
</Glance>

## Picture it

<Tr>
<En>

Think of the TypeScript compiler as a **translation office**, and `tsconfig.json` as the **job sheet** stapled to every order.

- "**Which documents?**" The sheet lists the folders to translate (`include`) and the ones to ignore (`exclude`).
- "**Into which dialect?**" Modern readers understand new slang; older readers need it spelled out the long way. That's `target`: newer targets keep modern syntax, older ones rewrite it.
- "**What does the reader already know?**" A browser reader knows about `document` and `window`; a server reader doesn't. That's `lib`.
- "**How picky should the proofreader be?**" `strict: true` is the senior editor who questions every vague sentence.
- "**Where do finished translations go?**" `outDir`. "**Include a glossary?**" `declaration` (`.d.ts`). "**Just proofread, don't translate**": `noEmit`.
- A company-wide **template job sheet** that each team copies and adjusts is `extends`.

</En>
<Ur>

TypeScript compiler ko **tarjume ka daftar** samjhein, aur `tsconfig.json` ko har order ke saath lage **job sheet** ko.

- "**Kaun se kaghzaat?**" Sheet un folders ki list deti hai jin ka tarjuma karna hai (`include`) aur jinhen chhorna hai (`exclude`).
- "**Kis lehje me?**" Naye parhne wale nayi bol chaal samajhte hain; purane parhne walon ko lambi tarah likh kar samjhana parta hai. Ye `target` hai: naye targets jadeed syntax rakhte hain, purane use dobara likhte hain.
- "**Parhne wala pehle se kya janta hai?**" Browser wala parhne wala `document` aur `window` janta hai; server wala nahi. Ye `lib` hai.
- "**Proofreader kitna nukta-cheen ho?**" `strict: true` wo senior editor hai jo har mubham jumle par sawal karta hai.
- "**Mukammal tarjume kahan jayen?**" `outDir`. "**Saath me farhang?**" `declaration` (`.d.ts`). "**Sirf proofread karo, tarjuma nahi**": `noEmit`.
- Company bhar ka **namoona job sheet** jise har team copy kar ke badalti hai `extends` hai.

</Ur>
</Tr>

## Words you'll see

<Tr>
<En>

| Word | What it means | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **`tsc`** | The TypeScript compiler command | `npx tsc` |
| **Compiler option** | One setting inside `compilerOptions` | `"strict": true` |
| **Target** | JavaScript version to output | `"es2022"` |
| **Downleveling** | Rewriting new syntax for older targets | `?.` → long `=== null` checks |
| **lib** | Built-in type definitions to include | `["es2022", "dom"]` |
| **Module system** | How files import each other | ESM (`import`) vs CommonJS (`require`) |
| **Module resolution** | How `import "./x"` is turned into a file | `nodenext`, `bundler` |
| **Emit** | Writing output files | `.js`, `.d.ts`, `.map` |
| **Declaration file** | A `.d.ts` file with only types | `price.d.ts` |
| **Source map** | Maps output lines back to source lines | `price.js.map` |
| **Strict mode** | A bundle of stricter checks | `strictNullChecks`, `noImplicitAny`… |
| **`extends`** | Inherit options from another tsconfig | `"./tsconfig.base.json"` |
| **Path alias** | A shortcut import prefix | `@/lib/db` |

</En>
<Ur>

| Lafz | Matlab | Misaal |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **`tsc`** | TypeScript compiler ki command | `npx tsc` |
| **Compiler option** | `compilerOptions` ke andar ek setting | `"strict": true` |
| **Target** | Output ka JavaScript version | `"es2022"` |
| **Downleveling** | Purane targets ke liye naya syntax dobara likhna | `?.` → lambe `=== null` checks |
| **lib** | Shamil karne wali built-in type definitions | `["es2022", "dom"]` |
| **Module system** | Files ek doosre ko kaise import karti hain | ESM (`import`) vs CommonJS (`require`) |
| **Module resolution** | `import "./x"` file me kaise badalta hai | `nodenext`, `bundler` |
| **Emit** | Output files likhna | `.js`, `.d.ts`, `.map` |
| **Declaration file** | Sirf types wali `.d.ts` file | `price.d.ts` |
| **Source map** | Output lines ko source lines se milata hai | `price.js.map` |
| **Strict mode** | Sakht checks ka majmua | `strictNullChecks`, `noImplicitAny`… |
| **`extends`** | Doosri tsconfig se options virse me lena | `"./tsconfig.base.json"` |
| **Path alias** | Import ka mukhtasar prefix | `@/lib/db` |

</Ur>
</Tr>

## Learn it step by step

<Walkthrough>

<Step title="Generate a starting tsconfig">

<Tr>
<En>
`npx tsc --init` writes a commented `tsconfig.json` with sensible modern defaults. Most lines are comments explaining options; let's filter them out to see what's actually switched on.
</En>
<Ur>
`npx tsc --init` tabsiron wali `tsconfig.json` likhta hai jis me samajhdar jadeed defaults hote hain. Zyada tar lines options samjhane wale comments hain; dekhte hain asal me kya on hai, comments chhaan kar.
</Ur>
</Tr>

```bash
mkdir -p init-demo && cd init-demo
npx tsc --init > /dev/null
grep -vE '^\s*//|^\s*$' tsconfig.json
```

```text output
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "module": "nodenext",
    "target": "esnext",
    "types": [],
    "sourceMap": true,
    "declaration": true,
    "declarationMap": true,
    "noUncheckedIndexedAccess": true,
    "exactOptionalPropertyTypes": true,
    "strict": true,
    "jsx": "react-jsx",
    "verbatimModuleSyntax": true,
    "isolatedModules": true,
    "noUncheckedSideEffectImports": true,
    "moduleDetection": "force",
    "skipLibCheck": true,
  }
}
```

<Happened>
<Tr>
<En>

- The file is JSON **with comments and trailing commas allowed** (TypeScript reads it leniently).
- The defaults are strict: `strict`, `noUncheckedIndexedAccess`, `exactOptionalPropertyTypes`. Good for new projects.
- `"types": []` means "don't automatically load every `@types/*` package". For Node.js code you'd add `"types": ["node"]` after `npm install -D @types/node`.
- The exact defaults change between TypeScript versions, so treat this as a starting point and understand each line you keep.

</En>
<Ur>

- File JSON hai **jis me comments aur aakhri commas ki ijazat hai** (TypeScript ise naram tareeqe se parhti hai).
- Defaults sakht hain: `strict`, `noUncheckedIndexedAccess`, `exactOptionalPropertyTypes`. Naye projects ke liye achha.
- `"types": []` ka matlab "har `@types/*` package khud load mat karo". Node.js code ke liye `npm install -D @types/node` ke baad `"types": ["node"]` jorein.
- Bilkul theek defaults TypeScript versions ke darmiyan badalte hain, isliye ise aaghaz samjhein aur jo line rakhein use samjhein.

</Ur>
</Tr>
</Happened>

</Step>

<Step title="target: which JavaScript comes out">

<Tr>
<En>
`target` decides the JavaScript version of the output. Newer syntax like `?.` and `??` is kept for modern targets and **rewritten** (downleveled) for older ones. Let's compile the same line twice.
</En>
<Ur>
`target` output ka JavaScript version tay karta hai. `?.` aur `??` jaisa naya syntax jadeed targets ke liye barqarar rehta hai aur purane targets ke liye **dobara likha** (downlevel) jata hai. Ek hi line do dafa compile karte hain.
</Ur>
</Tr>

```bash
mkdir -p flags && cd flags
cat > modern.ts <<'EOF'
type User = { address?: { city?: string } };
export const cityOf = (u: User) => u.address?.city ?? "unknown";
EOF
for tg in es2015 es2022; do
  echo "--- target $tg ---"
  npx tsc modern.ts --target $tg --module esnext --outDir out-$tg && cat out-$tg/modern.js
done
```

```text output
--- target es2015 ---
export const cityOf = (u) => { var _a; var _b; return (_b = (_a = u.address) === null || _a === void 0 ? void 0 : _a.city) !== null && _b !== void 0 ? _b : "unknown"; };
--- target es2022 ---
export const cityOf = (u) => u.address?.city ?? "unknown";
```

<Happened>
<Tr>
<En>

- For `es2015` (2015-era browsers), `?.` and `??` didn't exist yet, so tsc wrote the long equivalent.
- For `es2022` the output is almost identical to the input, minus the types.
- Choose the **oldest environment you must support**: Node 20+ handles `es2022` easily. In Next.js and Vite apps the bundler handles browser compatibility, so the tsconfig `target` matters less there.
- `target` does **not** add missing functions (like `Array.prototype.at` on old browsers). That needs a polyfill.

</En>
<Ur>

- `es2015` (2015 ke daur ke browsers) ke liye `?.` aur `??` abhi maujood nahi the, isliye tsc ne lamba barabar code likha.
- `es2022` ke liye output taqreeban input jaisa hai, types ke baghair.
- **Sab se purana mahaul jise support karna zaroori hai** chunein: Node 20+ `es2022` aasani se sambhalta hai. Next.js aur Vite apps me bundler browser compatibility sambhalta hai, isliye wahan tsconfig ka `target` kam ahem hai.
- `target` ghayab functions **nahi** jorta (jaise purane browsers par `Array.prototype.at`). Us ke liye polyfill chahiye.

</Ur>
</Tr>
</Happened>

</Step>

<Step title="lib: which built-in APIs exist">

<Tr>
<En>
`lib` tells TypeScript which built-in **types** exist: the language itself (`es2022`) and environments like the browser (`dom`). If `dom` isn't included, `document` and even `console` are unknown.
</En>
<Ur>
`lib` TypeScript ko batata hai ke kaun si built-in **types** maujood hain: khud zabaan (`es2022`) aur browser (`dom`) jaise mahaul. Agar `dom` shamil na ho to `document` aur `console` tak anjaan hain.
</Ur>
</Tr>

```bash
cd flags
cat > dom.ts <<'EOF'
const button = document.querySelector("button");
button?.addEventListener("click", () => console.log("hi"));
export {};
EOF
echo "--- lib es2022 only ---"
npx tsc --noEmit --strict --target es2022 --lib es2022 dom.ts
echo "--- lib es2022 + dom ---"
npx tsc --noEmit --strict --target es2022 --lib es2022,dom dom.ts && echo "no errors"
```

```text output
--- lib es2022 only ---
dom.ts(1,16): error TS2584: Cannot find name 'document'. Do you need to change your target library? Try changing the 'lib' compiler option to include 'dom'.
dom.ts(2,41): error TS2584: Cannot find name 'console'. Do you need to change your target library? Try changing the 'lib' compiler option to include 'dom'.
--- lib es2022 + dom ---
no errors
```

<Happened>
<Tr>
<En>

- `console` is defined by browsers (`dom`) and by Node (`@types/node`), not by the JavaScript language, which is why it's missing too.
- **Frontend code**: include `dom` (and `dom.iterable`). **Backend code**: leave `dom` out and add `"types": ["node"]`, so a stray `window` in server code becomes an error.
- If you don't set `lib`, TypeScript picks a default based on `target` (which includes `dom`).

</En>
<Ur>

- `console` browsers (`dom`) aur Node (`@types/node`) ki taraf se bayan hota hai, JavaScript zabaan ki taraf se nahi, isi liye ye bhi ghayab hai.
- **Frontend code**: `dom` (aur `dom.iterable`) shamil karein. **Backend code**: `dom` chhor dein aur `"types": ["node"]` jorein, taa ke server code me bhatka hua `window` error ban jaye.
- Agar `lib` set na karein to TypeScript `target` ke hisaab se default chunti hai (jis me `dom` shamil hai).

</Ur>
</Tr>
</Happened>

</Step>

<Step title="A real project: rootDir, outDir and include">

<Tr>
<En>
Now a small Node.js project. Sources live in `src`, compiled JavaScript goes to `dist`, and `"type": "module"` in `package.json` tells Node the output uses `import`/`export`. Running plain `npx tsc` (no file names) uses the tsconfig.
</En>
<Ur>
Ab ek chhota Node.js project. Sources `src` me hain, compile hua JavaScript `dist` me jata hai, aur `package.json` me `"type": "module"` Node ko batata hai ke output `import`/`export` istemal karta hai. Saada `npx tsc` (file names ke baghair) tsconfig istemal karta hai.
</Ur>
</Tr>

```bash
mkdir -p src
cat > src/price.ts <<'EOF'
export function withTax(amount: number, rate = 0.08): number {
  return Math.round(amount * (1 + rate) * 100) / 100;
}
EOF
cat > src/index.ts <<'EOF'
import { withTax } from "./price.js";
console.log("Total:", withTax(25));
EOF
echo '{ "type": "module" }' > package.json
cat > tsconfig.json <<'EOF'
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "target": "es2022",
    "module": "nodenext",
    "rootDir": "src",
    "outDir": "dist",
    "strict": true,
    "types": []
  },
  "include": ["src"]
}
EOF
npx tsc
find dist -type f | sort
node dist/index.js
```

```text output
dist/index.js
dist/price.js
Total: 27
```

<Happened>
<Tr>
<En>

- `include: ["src"]` picked up both files; `rootDir: "src"` + `outDir: "dist"` mirrored `src/price.ts` to `dist/price.js`.
- Node runs the **JavaScript in `dist`**, never the `.ts` files. Add `dist` to `.gitignore`; it's generated.
- Notice the import says `./price.js` even though the file is `price.ts`. That's the next step.
- With files in place, `npx tsc --watch` recompiles on every save.

</En>
<Ur>

- `include: ["src"]` ne dono files utha li; `rootDir: "src"` + `outDir: "dist"` ne `src/price.ts` ko `dist/price.js` me aaina kiya.
- Node **`dist` ka JavaScript** chalata hai, kabhi `.ts` files nahi. `dist` ko `.gitignore` me daalein; ye bana hua hai.
- Dhyan dein import `./price.js` kehta hai halanke file `price.ts` hai. Ye agla qadam hai.
- Files apni jagah hon to `npx tsc --watch` har save par dobara compile karta hai.

</Ur>
</Tr>
</Happened>

</Step>

<Step title="module nodenext and the .js extension">

<Tr>
<En>
With `module: "nodenext"`, TypeScript follows Node's real rules for ES modules: relative imports **must** include the file extension, and you write the extension of the **output** file (`.js`), because that's what Node will load.
</En>
<Ur>
`module: "nodenext"` ke saath TypeScript ES modules ke liye Node ke asli qawaid par chalti hai: relative imports me file ka extension **zaroori** hai, aur aap **output** file ka extension (`.js`) likhte hain, kyun ke Node wahi load karega.
</Ur>
</Tr>

```bash
cat > src/index.ts <<'EOF'
import { withTax } from "./price";
console.log("Total:", withTax(25));
EOF
npx tsc

cat > src/index.ts <<'EOF'
import { withTax } from "./price.js";
console.log("Total:", withTax(25));
EOF
npx tsc && echo "fixed: tsc is happy again"
```

```text output
src/index.ts(1,25): error TS2835: Relative import paths need explicit file extensions in ECMAScript imports when '--moduleResolution' is 'node16' or 'nodenext'. Did you mean './price.js'?
fixed: tsc is happy again
```

<Happened>
<Tr>
<En>

- Without the extension, Node itself would fail at runtime with `ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND`. TypeScript catches it at compile time instead, and even suggests the fix.
- In **bundler** projects (Next.js, Vite) the setting is `moduleResolution: "bundler"`, where extensionless imports are fine because the bundler resolves them.
- Rule of thumb: Node compiled by tsc → `nodenext` + `.js` extensions. Bundled app → `bundler`.

</En>
<Ur>

- Extension ke baghair khud Node runtime par `ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND` ke saath fail hota. TypeScript ise compile time par pakar leti hai, aur hal bhi batati hai.
- **Bundler** projects (Next.js, Vite) me setting `moduleResolution: "bundler"` hoti hai, jahan baghair extension imports theek hain kyun ke bundler unhen dhoondh leta hai.
- Aam usool: tsc se compile hone wala Node → `nodenext` + `.js` extensions. Bundle hone wali app → `bundler`.

</Ur>
</Tr>
</Happened>

</Step>

<Step title="strict: the most important switch">

<Tr>
<En>
`strict: true` turns on a family of checks, including `noImplicitAny` (parameters must have types) and `strictNullChecks` (`undefined` and `null` must be handled). Let's add a sloppy file and compare.
</En>
<Ur>
`strict: true` checks ka ek khandan on karta hai, jin me `noImplicitAny` (parameters ki types zaroori) aur `strictNullChecks` (`undefined` aur `null` sambhalna zaroori) shamil hain. Ek laaparwah file jor kar muqabla karte hain.
</Ur>
</Tr>

```bash
cat > src/loose.ts <<'EOF'
function total(items) {
  return items.reduce((s, i) => s + i.price, 0);
}
function findName(names: string[], i: number) {
  const name: string = names.find((n) => n.length > i);
  return name;
}
const prices: Record<string, number> = { mug: 12 };
const lamp = prices["lamp"];
console.log(lamp.toFixed(2));
EOF
echo "--- strict: true ---"
npx tsc --noEmit
echo "--- strict: false ---"
npx tsc --noEmit --strict false && echo "no errors (bugs still there)"
```

```text output
--- strict: true ---
src/loose.ts(1,16): error TS7006: Parameter 'items' implicitly has an 'any' type.
src/loose.ts(2,24): error TS7006: Parameter 's' implicitly has an 'any' type.
src/loose.ts(2,27): error TS7006: Parameter 'i' implicitly has an 'any' type.
src/loose.ts(5,9): error TS2322: Type 'string | undefined' is not assignable to type 'string'.
  Type 'undefined' is not assignable to type 'string'.
--- strict: false ---
no errors (bugs still there)
```

<Happened>
<Tr>
<En>

- With `strict`, untyped parameters are errors (`noImplicitAny`), and `find` possibly returning `undefined` is caught (`strictNullChecks`).
- With `strict: false`, the same file passes, and `findName` can return `undefined` while claiming `string`. TypeScript becomes "JavaScript with optional hints".
- Command-line flags (`--strict false`) override the tsconfig, which is handy for experiments.
- **Always start new projects strict.** Migrating an old JavaScript project? Turn options on one at a time.

</En>
<Ur>

- `strict` ke saath baghair type parameters errors hain (`noImplicitAny`), aur `find` ka shayad `undefined` wapas karna pakra jata hai (`strictNullChecks`).
- `strict: false` ke saath wahi file paas ho jati hai, aur `findName` `string` ka daawa karte hue `undefined` wapas kar sakta hai. TypeScript "ikhtiyari ishaaron wala JavaScript" ban jati hai.
- Command-line flags (`--strict false`) tsconfig par ghalib aate hain, jo tajurbon ke liye kaam ka hai.
- **Naye projects hamesha strict shuru karein.** Purana JavaScript project muntaqil kar rahe hain? Options ek ek kar ke on karein.

</Ur>
</Tr>
</Happened>

</Step>

<Step title="noUncheckedIndexedAccess: lookups may be missing">

<Tr>
<En>
Even `strict` assumes `prices["lamp"]` is a `number`. But the key might not exist. `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` adds `| undefined` to every index lookup, so line 10 of the same file is caught.
</En>
<Ur>
`strict` bhi maanta hai ke `prices["lamp"]` `number` hai. Magar key shayad maujood na ho. `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` har index talaash me `| undefined` jor deta hai, isliye usi file ki line 10 pakri jati hai.
</Ur>
</Tr>

```bash
npx tsc --noEmit --noUncheckedIndexedAccess | grep "loose.ts(10"
rm src/loose.ts
```

```text output
src/loose.ts(10,13): error TS18048: 'lamp' is possibly 'undefined'.
```

<Happened>
<Tr>
<En>

- `prices` has no `lamp`, so `lamp.toFixed(2)` would crash with "Cannot read properties of undefined". Only this flag catches it.
- It also applies to arrays: `names[5]` becomes `string | undefined`. That's more `if` checks, but each one is a real crash prevented.
- Not part of `strict` because it makes existing code noisier, but `tsc --init` now turns it on, and it's worth it in new code.
- (We deleted `loose.ts` so the next steps compile cleanly.)

</En>
<Ur>

- `prices` me `lamp` nahi, isliye `lamp.toFixed(2)` "Cannot read properties of undefined" ke saath crash karta. Sirf ye flag ise pakarta hai.
- Ye arrays par bhi lagta hai: `names[5]` `string | undefined` ban jata hai. Zyada `if` checks, magar har ek asli crash se bachata hai.
- `strict` ka hissa nahi kyun ke ye maujooda code me shor barhata hai, magar `tsc --init` ab ise on karta hai, aur naye code me ye faidemand hai.
- (Humne `loose.ts` mita di taa ke agle qadam saaf compile hon.)

</Ur>
</Tr>
</Happened>

</Step>

<Step title="Output extras: declarations, source maps and noEmit">

<Tr>
<En>
`declaration` writes `.d.ts` files (just the types) so other projects can use your code with types. `sourceMap` writes `.map` files so debuggers and stack traces point at your `.ts` lines. `noEmit` writes nothing, only checks.
</En>
<Ur>
`declaration` `.d.ts` files (sirf types) likhta hai taa ke doosre projects aap ka code types ke saath istemal kar sakein. `sourceMap` `.map` files likhta hai taa ke debuggers aur stack traces aap ki `.ts` lines ki taraf ishara karein. `noEmit` kuch nahi likhta, sirf check karta hai.
</Ur>
</Tr>

```bash
rm -rf dist
npx tsc --declaration --sourceMap
find dist -type f | sort
echo "--- dist/price.d.ts ---"
cat dist/price.d.ts
echo "--- last line of dist/price.js ---"
tail -1 dist/price.js; echo
rm -rf dist && npx tsc --noEmit && echo "noEmit: checked, dist exists? $(test -d dist && echo yes || echo no)"
```

```text output
dist/index.d.ts
dist/index.js
dist/index.js.map
dist/price.d.ts
dist/price.js
dist/price.js.map
--- dist/price.d.ts ---
export declare function withTax(amount: number, rate?: number): number;
--- last line of dist/price.js ---
//# sourceMappingURL=price.js.map
noEmit: checked, dist exists? no
```

<Happened>
<Tr>
<En>

- The `.d.ts` is the "glossary": `withTax(amount: number, rate?: number): number`, with the default value turned into an optional parameter. npm packages ship these so you get autocomplete.
- The comment at the end of `price.js` tells debuggers where its source map is (Debugging JavaScript lesson).
- `noEmit` is what Next.js and Vite projects use: the bundler (SWC, esbuild) turns TS into JS, and `tsc --noEmit` (often `npm run typecheck`) is used only to check types, for example in CI.

</En>
<Ur>

- `.d.ts` "farhang" hai: `withTax(amount: number, rate?: number): number`, default value ikhtiyari parameter me badal gayi. npm packages yahi bhejte hain taa ke aap ko autocomplete mile.
- `price.js` ke aakhir ka comment debuggers ko batata hai ke us ka source map kahan hai (Debugging JavaScript lesson).
- `noEmit` Next.js aur Vite projects istemal karte hain: bundler (SWC, esbuild) TS ko JS me badalta hai, aur `tsc --noEmit` (aksar `npm run typecheck`) sirf types check karne ke liye hota hai, maslan CI me.

</Ur>
</Tr>
</Happened>

</Step>

<Step title="extends and --showConfig">

<Tr>
<En>
Teams keep shared settings in one base file and `extends` it. Options in the child **override** the base. `npx tsc --showConfig` prints the final merged result, which is the fastest way to answer "what setting is actually in effect?".
</En>
<Ur>
Teams mushtarka settings ek base file me rakhti hain aur use `extends` karti hain. Child ke options base par **ghalib** aate hain. `npx tsc --showConfig` aakhri mila hua nateeja print karta hai, jo "asal me kaun si setting chal rahi hai?" ka sab se tez jawab hai.
</Ur>
</Tr>

```bash
cat > tsconfig.base.json <<'EOF'
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "strict": true,
    "noUncheckedIndexedAccess": true,
    "target": "es2020",
    "skipLibCheck": true
  }
}
EOF
cat > tsconfig.json <<'EOF'
{
  "extends": "./tsconfig.base.json",
  "compilerOptions": {
    "target": "es2022",
    "module": "nodenext",
    "rootDir": "src",
    "outDir": "dist",
    "types": []
  },
  "include": ["src"]
}
EOF
npx tsc --showConfig | sed -n '/"compilerOptions"/,/^    }/p'
```

```text output
    "compilerOptions": {
        "module": "nodenext",
        "noUncheckedIndexedAccess": true,
        "outDir": "./dist",
        "rootDir": "./src",
        "skipLibCheck": true,
        "strict": true,
        "target": "es2022",
        "types": [],
        "moduleResolution": "nodenext",
        "moduleDetection": "force"
    },
```

<Happened>
<Tr>
<En>

- `strict`, `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` and `skipLibCheck` came from the base. `target` is `es2022` because the child overrode the base's `es2020`.
- `moduleResolution` and `moduleDetection` weren't written anywhere: `--showConfig` reveals values **implied** by `module: "nodenext"`.
- `extends` can also point to an npm package, such as `@tsconfig/node22`, a community-maintained base config for each Node version.
- Note that `include`, `files` and `exclude` are **replaced**, not merged, when a child sets them.

</En>
<Ur>

- `strict`, `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` aur `skipLibCheck` base se aaye. `target` `es2022` hai kyun ke child ne base ka `es2020` badal diya.
- `moduleResolution` aur `moduleDetection` kahin likhe nahi gaye: `--showConfig` wo values dikhata hai jo `module: "nodenext"` se **khud lagu** hoti hain.
- `extends` npm package ki taraf bhi ishara kar sakta hai, jaise `@tsconfig/node22`, har Node version ke liye community ki banayi base config.
- Dhyan dein ke child agar `include`, `files` aur `exclude` set kare to ye **badal** jate hain, milte nahi.

</Ur>
</Tr>
</Happened>

</Step>

<Step title="paths aliases: types only, not runtime">

<Tr>
<En>
`paths` lets you write `@/price.js` instead of `../../price.js`. But it only teaches **the type checker** where to look. tsc does **not** rewrite the import in the output, so plain Node can't find it.
</En>
<Ur>
`paths` aap ko `../../price.js` ke bajaye `@/price.js` likhne deta hai. Magar ye sirf **type checker** ko batata hai ke kahan dekhna hai. tsc output me import **dobara nahi** likhta, isliye saada Node use nahi dhoondh pata.
</Ur>
</Tr>

```bash
cat > src/index.ts <<'EOF'
import { withTax } from "@/price.js";
console.log("Total:", withTax(25));
EOF
cat > tsconfig.json <<'EOF'
{
  "extends": "./tsconfig.base.json",
  "compilerOptions": {
    "target": "es2022",
    "module": "nodenext",
    "rootDir": "src",
    "outDir": "dist",
    "types": [],
    "paths": { "@/*": ["./src/*"] }
  },
  "include": ["src"]
}
EOF
npx tsc && echo "tsc: no errors"
grep import dist/index.js
node dist/index.js 2>&1 | grep -m1 -o "Cannot find package '[^']*'"
```

```text output
tsc: no errors
import { withTax } from "@/price.js";
Cannot find package '@/price.js'
```

<Happened>
<Tr>
<En>

- Type checking passed and the editor would autocomplete `@/`. But the output still says `"@/price.js"`, and Node treats that as an npm package name.
- **In Next.js and Vite this just works**, because the bundler reads `paths` and rewrites imports.
- For plain Node, use Node's own **`imports`** field in `package.json` (`"#lib/*": "./dist/*"`, imported as `#lib/price.js`), which both Node and TypeScript understand, or a tool that rewrites paths after compiling.

</En>
<Ur>

- Type checking paas hui aur editor `@/` autocomplete karta. Magar output ab bhi `"@/price.js"` kehta hai, aur Node use npm package ka naam samajhta hai.
- **Next.js aur Vite me ye seedha chalta hai**, kyun ke bundler `paths` parh kar imports dobara likhta hai.
- Saade Node ke liye `package.json` me Node ka apna **`imports`** field istemal karein (`"#lib/*": "./dist/*"`, `#lib/price.js` ke taur par import), jise Node aur TypeScript dono samajhte hain, ya aisa tool jo compile ke baad paths dobara likhe.

</Ur>
</Tr>
</Happened>

</Step>

<Step title="Reading a Next.js tsconfig">

<Tr>
<En>

Here's a typical Next.js `tsconfig.json`. You can now read every line:

```text
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "target": "ES2017",              // output level for tsc (SWC does the real build)
    "lib": ["dom", "dom.iterable", "esnext"], // browser + latest language types
    "allowJs": true,                 // .js files can live alongside .ts
    "skipLibCheck": true,            // don't re-check node_modules types
    "strict": true,                  // all the important checks
    "noEmit": true,                  // tsc only checks; Next.js builds
    "esModuleInterop": true,         // smoother default imports from CommonJS packages
    "module": "esnext",
    "moduleResolution": "bundler",   // extensionless imports, resolved by the bundler
    "resolveJsonModule": true,       // import data from "./x.json"
    "isolatedModules": true,         // every file can be compiled on its own (SWC)
    "jsx": "preserve",               // leave JSX for Next.js to transform
    "incremental": true,             // cache for faster re-checks
    "plugins": [{ "name": "next" }], // editor plugin for Next.js-specific hints
    "paths": { "@/*": ["./*"] }      // import "@/components/button"
  },
  "include": ["next-env.d.ts", "**/*.ts", "**/*.tsx", ".next/types/**/*.ts"],
  "exclude": ["node_modules"]
}
```

</En>
<Ur>

Ye ek aam Next.js `tsconfig.json` hai. Ab aap har line parh sakte hain:

```text
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "target": "ES2017",              // tsc ka output level (asal build SWC karta hai)
    "lib": ["dom", "dom.iterable", "esnext"], // browser + taaza tareen zabaan ki types
    "allowJs": true,                 // .js files .ts ke saath reh sakti hain
    "skipLibCheck": true,            // node_modules ki types dobara check mat karo
    "strict": true,                  // tamam ahem checks
    "noEmit": true,                  // tsc sirf check karta hai; Next.js banata hai
    "esModuleInterop": true,         // CommonJS packages se aasan default imports
    "module": "esnext",
    "moduleResolution": "bundler",   // baghair extension imports, bundler dhoondhta hai
    "resolveJsonModule": true,       // "./x.json" se data import
    "isolatedModules": true,         // har file akeli compile ho sakti hai (SWC)
    "jsx": "preserve",               // JSX Next.js ke badalne ke liye chhor do
    "incremental": true,             // tez dobara check ke liye cache
    "plugins": [{ "name": "next" }], // Next.js ke khaas ishaaron ka editor plugin
    "paths": { "@/*": ["./*"] }      // import "@/components/button"
  },
  "include": ["next-env.d.ts", "**/*.ts", "**/*.tsx", ".next/types/**/*.ts"],
  "exclude": ["node_modules"]
}
```

</Ur>
</Tr>

<Happened>
<Tr>
<En>

- `noEmit` + `moduleResolution: "bundler"` + `jsx: "preserve"` all say the same thing: **Next.js builds, tsc only checks**.
- `isolatedModules` exists because SWC compiles each file separately and can't do things that need the whole program (like `const enum`).
- When Next.js updates, it may edit this file for you; read the diff rather than fighting it.

</En>
<Ur>

- `noEmit` + `moduleResolution: "bundler"` + `jsx: "preserve"` sab ek hi baat kehte hain: **Next.js banata hai, tsc sirf check karta hai**.
- `isolatedModules` is liye hai ke SWC har file alag compile karta hai aur wo kaam nahi kar sakta jin ke liye poora program chahiye (jaise `const enum`).
- Jab Next.js update ho, ye aap ke liye is file me tabdeeli kar sakta hai; is se larne ke bajaye diff parhein.

</Ur>
</Tr>
</Happened>

</Step>

</Walkthrough>

## Common mistakes

<Compare>
<Bad title="Turning strict off to make errors disappear">

```text
// 200 errors after enabling strict…
"strict": false
// …now 0 errors, and every one of those bugs is still in the code
```

</Bad>
<Good title="Fix gradually, keep the safety">

```text
"strict": true
// fix errors folder by folder; for a big migration, temporarily use
// // @ts-expect-error  with a TODO comment on the hardest lines,
// so new code is always checked strictly
```

</Good>
</Compare>

<Compare>
<Bad title="Browser types in server code">

```text
// API project tsconfig
"lib": ["es2022", "dom"]
// a copied line using window.localStorage compiles,
// then crashes on the server: "window is not defined"
```

</Bad>
<Good title="Only the environment you run in">

```text
// API project tsconfig
"lib": ["es2022"],
"types": ["node"]
// window and localStorage are now compile errors in server code
```

</Good>
</Compare>

<Tr>
<En>

More mistakes to avoid:

- **Running the `.ts` files with plain `node`** after compiling with tsc: run the files in `outDir`.
- **Missing `.js` extensions** with `nodenext`, or adding them in a bundler project where they aren't needed.
- **Expecting `paths` to work at runtime** without a bundler or Node's `imports` field.
- **Committing `dist`**: it's generated; build it in CI or on deploy.
- **Copying a tsconfig from another project type** (a Next.js config into a Node API, or the reverse).
- **Passing file names to `tsc` and wondering why the tsconfig was ignored**: `tsc file.ts` doesn't use the project config.

</En>
<Ur>

Bachne wali mazeed ghaltiyan:

- tsc se compile karne ke baad **`.ts` files saade `node` se chalana**: `outDir` wali files chalayen.
- `nodenext` ke saath **`.js` extensions bhoolna**, ya bundler project me lagana jahan zaroorat nahi.
- Bundler ya Node ke `imports` field ke baghair **`paths` ke runtime par chalne ki umeed**.
- **`dist` commit karna**: ye bana hua hai; ise CI ya deploy par banayen.
- **Doosri qism ke project ki tsconfig copy karna** (Next.js ki config Node API me, ya ulta).
- **`tsc` ko file names dena aur hairan hona ke tsconfig kyun nazarandaz hui**: `tsc file.ts` project config istemal nahi karta.

</Ur>
</Tr>

## Try it yourself

<Challenge title="Spot the right settings">

<Tr>
<En>
For each project, write the key options: (1) a Vite + React app; (2) an Express API compiled with tsc to `dist` and run with `node dist/server.js`; (3) a small npm library that other TypeScript projects will install.
</En>
<Ur>
Har project ke liye ahem options likhein: (1) Vite + React app; (2) Express API jo tsc se `dist` me compile ho aur `node dist/server.js` se chale; (3) chhoti npm library jise doosre TypeScript projects install karenge.
</Ur>
</Tr>

<Solution>

<Tr>
<En>

```text
(1) Vite + React
  "strict": true, "noEmit": true, "jsx": "react-jsx",
  "module": "esnext", "moduleResolution": "bundler",
  "lib": ["es2022", "dom", "dom.iterable"], "isolatedModules": true

(2) Express API
  "strict": true, "module": "nodenext", "target": "es2022",
  "rootDir": "src", "outDir": "dist", "types": ["node"], "sourceMap": true
  (+ "type": "module" in package.json and .js extensions in imports)

(3) npm library
  "strict": true, "declaration": true, "declarationMap": true,
  "outDir": "dist", "module": "nodenext"
  (+ "types": "./dist/index.d.ts" in package.json)
```

</En>
<Ur>

```text
(1) Vite + React
  "strict": true, "noEmit": true, "jsx": "react-jsx",
  "module": "esnext", "moduleResolution": "bundler",
  "lib": ["es2022", "dom", "dom.iterable"], "isolatedModules": true

(2) Express API
  "strict": true, "module": "nodenext", "target": "es2022",
  "rootDir": "src", "outDir": "dist", "types": ["node"], "sourceMap": true
  (+ package.json me "type": "module" aur imports me .js extensions)

(3) npm library
  "strict": true, "declaration": true, "declarationMap": true,
  "outDir": "dist", "module": "nodenext"
  (+ package.json me "types": "./dist/index.d.ts")
```

</Ur>
</Tr>

</Solution>

</Challenge>

<Challenge title="Make it stricter">

<Tr>
<En>
Compile this file with `--strict` alone, then add `--noUncheckedIndexedAccess`, and fix the code so both pass.

```text
const scores: number[] = [90, 75];
const third = scores[2];
console.log("Third score:", third.toFixed(0));
```

</En>
<Ur>
Is file ko pehle sirf `--strict` se compile karein, phir `--noUncheckedIndexedAccess` jorein, aur code theek karein taa ke dono paas hon.

```text
const scores: number[] = [90, 75];
const third = scores[2];
console.log("Third score:", third.toFixed(0));
```

</Ur>
</Tr>

<Solution>

```bash
mkdir -p challenge && cd challenge
cat > scores.ts <<'EOF'
const scores: number[] = [90, 75];
const third = scores[2];
console.log("Third score:", third.toFixed(0));
EOF
echo "--- strict ---"
npx tsc --noEmit --strict --ignoreConfig scores.ts && echo "passes, but crashes at runtime"
echo "--- strict + noUncheckedIndexedAccess ---"
npx tsc --noEmit --strict --noUncheckedIndexedAccess --ignoreConfig scores.ts
cat > scores.ts <<'EOF'
const scores: number[] = [90, 75];
const third = scores[2];
console.log("Third score:", third === undefined ? "none yet" : third.toFixed(0));
EOF
npx tsc --noEmit --strict --noUncheckedIndexedAccess --ignoreConfig scores.ts && echo "fixed"
```

```text output
--- strict ---
passes, but crashes at runtime
--- strict + noUncheckedIndexedAccess ---
scores.ts(3,29): error TS18048: 'third' is possibly 'undefined'.
fixed
```

<Tr>
<En>
`--ignoreConfig` tells newer tsc versions to compile just this file even though a `tsconfig.json` exists in a parent folder (older versions simply ignore the config when you pass file names).
</En>
<Ur>
`--ignoreConfig` naye tsc versions ko batata hai ke parent folder me `tsconfig.json` hone ke bawajood sirf ye file compile karo (purane versions file names dene par config khud hi nazarandaz kar dete hain).
</Ur>
</Tr>

</Solution>

</Challenge>

## Quick quiz

<Quiz>
<Question q="What does target control?">
<Option>Which files are compiled</Option>
<Option correct>The JavaScript version of the output</Option>
<Option>Which browser APIs exist</Option>
<Explanation>Older targets rewrite newer syntax such as optional chaining.</Explanation>
</Question>
<Question q="Why does 'Cannot find name document' appear?">
<Option>document is misspelled</Option>
<Option correct>The dom library isn't included in lib</Option>
<Option>strict mode forbids document</Option>
<Explanation>Browser APIs come from the dom lib.</Explanation>
</Question>
<Question q="With module nodenext, how do you import src/price.ts from src/index.ts?">
<Option>from "./price"</Option>
<Option>from "./price.ts"</Option>
<Option correct>from "./price.js"</Option>
<Explanation>You write the extension of the output file that Node will load.</Explanation>
</Question>
<Question q="What does noEmit do?">
<Option>Hides errors</Option>
<Option correct>Type-checks without writing any output files</Option>
<Option>Deletes the dist folder</Option>
<Explanation>Used when a bundler builds the code and tsc only checks it.</Explanation>
</Question>
<Question q="Why can an import using a paths alias fail in plain Node after tsc compiles it?">
<Option>paths is deprecated</Option>
<Option correct>tsc doesn't rewrite the import; paths only affects type checking</Option>
<Option>Node doesn't support ES modules</Option>
<Explanation>Bundlers rewrite aliases; plain Node needs package.json imports or a rewrite step.</Explanation>
</Question>
</Quiz>

## Remember

<Takeaways>
<Tr>
<En>

- `tsconfig.json` answers: which files, how strict, what JavaScript, where output goes.
- `target` = output language version (downlevels new syntax, no polyfills); `lib` = which built-in types exist (`dom` for browsers, `@types/node` for Node).
- `module: "nodenext"` needs `.js` extensions in relative imports; bundler projects use `moduleResolution: "bundler"`.
- `rootDir` → `outDir` mirrors `src` into `dist`; run the output, not the `.ts`.
- Keep `strict: true`; add `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` for safer lookups.
- `declaration` for libraries, `sourceMap` for debugging, `noEmit` when a bundler builds.
- `extends` shares settings; `npx tsc --showConfig` shows the final result.
- `paths` aliases are for types; runtime needs a bundler or Node's `imports`.

</En>
<Ur>

- `tsconfig.json` jawab deti hai: kaun si files, kitni sakhti, kaun sa JavaScript, output kahan jaye.
- `target` = output zabaan ka version (naya syntax downlevel karta hai, polyfills nahi); `lib` = kaun si built-in types maujood hain (browsers ke liye `dom`, Node ke liye `@types/node`).
- `module: "nodenext"` ko relative imports me `.js` extensions chahiyen; bundler projects `moduleResolution: "bundler"` istemal karte hain.
- `rootDir` → `outDir` `src` ko `dist` me aaina karta hai; output chalayen, `.ts` nahi.
- `strict: true` rakhein; mehfooz talaash ke liye `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` jorein.
- Libraries ke liye `declaration`, debugging ke liye `sourceMap`, bundler banaye to `noEmit`.
- `extends` settings baant'ta hai; `npx tsc --showConfig` aakhri nateeja dikhata hai.
- `paths` aliases types ke liye hain; runtime ko bundler ya Node ka `imports` chahiye.

</Ur>
</Tr>
</Takeaways>

## Go deeper

<Tr>
<En>
The sections below are for when you're comfortable with the basics, or getting ready for interviews.
</En>
<Ur>
Neeche ke hisse tab ke liye hain jab basics achi tarah samajh aa jayen, ya interview ki tayyari ho.
</Ur>
</Tr>

<DeepDive title="More tsconfig options worth knowing">

**What `strict` includes.** `noImplicitAny`, `strictNullChecks`, `strictFunctionTypes`, `strictBindCallApply`, `strictPropertyInitialization`, `noImplicitThis`, `useUnknownInCatchVariables`, `alwaysStrict`, and newer ones as TypeScript adds them. You can turn any of them off individually after `strict: true`.

**`exactOptionalPropertyTypes`.** Makes `nickname?: string` mean "missing or a string", not "or explicitly `undefined`". Stricter, but some libraries' types don't expect it.

**`verbatimModuleSyntax`.** Forces `import type { X }` for type-only imports, so tools that compile one file at a time know which imports to drop.

**`isolatedModules`.** Errors on features that need the whole program to compile (like `const enum` across files, or re-exporting types without `export type`). Required by SWC, esbuild and Babel setups.

**`allowImportingTsExtensions` + `rewriteRelativeImportExtensions`.** For running `.ts` directly with Node, you can import `./price.ts`; TypeScript 5.7+ can rewrite those to `.js` when emitting.

**`incremental` and `composite`.** Cache build info in `.tsbuildinfo` for faster rebuilds; `composite` + `references` split a monorepo into projects built with `tsc --build`.

**`types` and `typeRoots`.** Control which `@types/*` packages load automatically. An empty array gives a clean global scope; add what you need (`"node"`, `"vitest/globals"`).

**TypeScript 7 (native).** The Go-based compiler is much faster and stricter about some config situations, for example refusing to silently ignore a tsconfig when you pass file names (`TS5112`) unless you use `--ignoreConfig`.

</DeepDive>

<DeepDive title="Real world: the deploy that couldn't find its own files">

A team moved their Express API from CommonJS to ES modules. Locally everything worked with `ts-node`. In production the container started, then crashed immediately: `ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND: Cannot find module '/app/dist/routes/users'`.

Three settings were involved:

1. `module` was still `"commonjs"` in an older base config pulled in through `extends`, while `package.json` said `"type": "module"`. Running `npx tsc --showConfig` revealed the inherited value in seconds.
2. After switching to `"nodenext"`, tsc reported 140 imports without `.js` extensions, the exact files Node couldn't find. A codemod added them.
3. `@/` path aliases worked in development because `ts-node` used a paths plugin, but compiled output still contained `@/services/mail`. They replaced the aliases with `package.json` `imports` (`#services/*`).

They added `npm run build && node dist/server.js --smoke-test` to CI, so the production start-up is tested before every deploy.

</DeepDive>

<DeepDive title="Security lens">

- **`sourceMap` in production frontends** exposes your original source code to anyone. Upload maps privately to your error tracker, or don't serve them publicly.
- **`skipLibCheck: true`** skips checking type definitions in `node_modules`. It's standard practice for speed, but remember it doesn't check those types are correct; it says nothing about package safety either way.
- **Don't let `allowJs` + loose settings hide untyped code** in security-sensitive paths (auth, payments). Keep those in strict `.ts`.
- **`strict` + `noUncheckedIndexedAccess`** prevent whole classes of crashes that can become denial-of-service bugs (a missing key in a request crashing a worker).
- **Keep `outDir` out of version control** so stale compiled files, perhaps including removed debug endpoints, never get deployed by accident.

</DeepDive>

<DeepDive title="Interview questions">

<QA q="What is the difference between target and lib?">
target sets the JavaScript version of the emitted code, which decides whether newer syntax is rewritten. lib sets which built-in type declarations are available to the checker, such as ES2022 features or browser DOM APIs. lib does not add runtime polyfills.
</QA>

<QA q="Why do imports need .js extensions with module nodenext?">
nodenext follows Node's ES module resolution, which requires explicit file extensions for relative imports. Since Node loads the compiled JavaScript, the import must name the output file's extension, which TypeScript maps back to the .ts source while checking.
</QA>

<QA q="What does strict do?">
It enables a group of stricter type-checking options, including noImplicitAny and strictNullChecks, so that untyped values and possible null or undefined values must be handled. New TypeScript projects should enable it.
</QA>

<QA q="When would you use noEmit?">
When another tool such as a bundler, Next.js, Vite or a test runner transpiles the TypeScript, so tsc is only used to type-check, typically in CI or a typecheck script.
</QA>

<QA q="Why might a paths alias compile but fail at runtime?">
paths only tells the type checker how to resolve module names; tsc does not rewrite import specifiers in the output. A bundler, a post-build rewrite, or Node's package.json imports field is needed for the runtime to resolve the alias.
</QA>

</DeepDive>

<DeepDive title="All key terms">

<Terms>
  <Term name="tsconfig.json">The configuration file for a TypeScript project.</Term>
  <Term name="compilerOptions">The section of tsconfig holding compiler settings.</Term>
  <Term name="target">The ECMAScript version of emitted JavaScript.</Term>
  <Term name="lib">The set of built-in type declaration files available.</Term>
  <Term name="module">The module format of emitted code and related resolution behaviour.</Term>
  <Term name="moduleResolution">The algorithm used to find imported modules.</Term>
  <Term name="rootDir">The root folder of the source files.</Term>
  <Term name="outDir">The folder where emitted files are written.</Term>
  <Term name="strict">A switch enabling the main strict type-checking options.</Term>
  <Term name="noUncheckedIndexedAccess">Adds undefined to the type of index access results.</Term>
  <Term name="declaration">Emits .d.ts type declaration files.</Term>
  <Term name="sourceMap">Emits maps from output back to the source.</Term>
  <Term name="noEmit">Type-check only, without writing output.</Term>
  <Term name="extends">Inherits settings from another configuration file.</Term>
  <Term name="paths">Maps import specifiers to locations for type checking.</Term>
</Terms>

</DeepDive>

<DeepDive title="More practice">

1. Run `npx tsc --init` in an empty folder and look up every option it enables.
2. Compile the same file with `target` `es5`, `es2015` and `es2022` and compare the output for `class`, `async` and `?.`.
3. Create a Node project with `nodenext`, then try running the `.ts` file with `node --experimental-strip-types` and `noEmit`.
4. Set up a `tsconfig.base.json` with two packages extending it, and check each with `--showConfig`.
5. Replace a `paths` alias with Node's `package.json` `imports` field and confirm the compiled code runs.
6. Open your current project's tsconfig and explain every line to a friend.

</DeepDive>
